title: Biological macromolecules
note: Life's four large molecule classes are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Most are polymers: dehydration synthesis links monomers and releases water, and hydrolysis adds water to split them. A protein's amino acid sequence determines how it folds, and its shape determines its function.

read.title: Building big molecules from small parts
text: Cells build their largest molecules the way a train is built from cars. Small units called monomers are joined into long chains called polymers. Each link forms by dehydration synthesis: one monomer gives up a hydroxyl group, the other a hydrogen, and a molecule of water is released. Reversing the process, hydrolysis, uses water to break the link. Digestion is largely hydrolysis.

Carbohydrates follow this pattern. Glucose units linked one way form starch, a plant energy store, or glycogen, the animal version. Linked a slightly different way, glucose forms cellulose, the tough fiber of plant cell walls that most animals cannot digest.

Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Twenty amino acids, differing only in their side chains, can be arranged in a vast number of sequences. The sequence is the primary structure, and it determines how the chain coils into helices and sheets and then folds into a final three-dimensional shape. Shape is everything: if heat or extreme pH unfolds a protein, it usually stops working.
Lipids are the exception. Fats and phospholipids are assembled from glycerol and fatty acids, but they are not long chains of repeating monomers.

q.q: What is released each time dehydration synthesis forms a link?
